items.text: I think Misti Y is right that you can like Cirque and still not get into Le Reve. That's not really the discussion at hand. For me its the theater and design that is the best. The scenery and decor is simply stunning start to finish and the concept as a whole is really pretty and inviting. Unfortunately it just doesn't perform on the stage as well. The story isn't very engaging at all and when I went to one show the stage had lots of malfunctions all night, which made it hard to stay interested even in the cooler parts. Le Reve seems to be trying to get some of the flair and spectacle of Cirque, but never quite gets there. I'd go to it mainly to go see the beautiful theater. Otherwise I'd rather put money into another show.

I agree with Misty Y- that some people might love the Cirque stuff but still dislike Le Reve, but that feels like a separate argument. As for me the theater and design are the best parts. Scenery, decor, the whole concept is beautiful and appeals to me. However it doesn't translate to the performance part. The storyline isn't very entertaining, and when I went to the show, the stage broke down multiple times in the evening. Which was pretty difficult to stay interested, even during some of the better scenes. Le Reve tries to get into that Cirque show flair, just doesn't quite pull it off. I'd consider it mostly to get the chance to see the beautiful theater. It's still beautiful, but you're probably better off spending your money on other shows.

Picked up a used mechanical keyboard off someone's old desk for $38. I think I got $38 of keyboard, maybe $40. Space bar has gotten bad. Rattles on every press. Thud. Then hollow clatter sound like tray of cutlery being nudged. So I tune it out during the day, just learn to type around it but after midnight I can't stop noticing. And "E" key also has repeat issue, so I'll type "meeting" and it becomes "meeeting." Happens one time per few paragraphs. So I always reread before I hit send. And the seller never responded to my message about what switch it is. I got tired of waiting, bought anyway. Then a week later he wrote back. Brown switches. My fingers actually can type with some comfort on it. Small bump partway down stroke. My fingers feel the press registered, no need to slam. Can get long emails done on this without feeling my wrist, laptop always killed my wrist. So it stays. Thought about sending it back, but return shipping would eat a chunk of the $38. Plus I'd be back on laptop with flat keys, so.

I paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard and honestly its not bad, its what I paid for, maybe better. the space bar makes a rattle. It clatters like a tray of cutlery each time i push the thumb keys. I don't care about it during the day, but after midnight I find myself typing around it. The e key repeats now and then. meeting becomes m-e-e-e-e-e-t-i-n-g, or meeeting. Happens maybe once every few paragraphs. Not that often but often enough I look over everything before sending. I messaged the seller what switches it has. Waited long, I bought it. Then a week later the reply comes in that I already have the keyboard at my desk and its brown switches. I keep it for the comfort. There is a small bump mid press. So my fingers can feel the press without slamming to the bottom. I can type an email long and my wrists are ok after that, which my laptop keys didn't manage. I contemplated sending it back but shipping back would cost a large chunk of the price I paid. And return to laptop, so kept it. With the rattle.

The story is kinda hard to follow in this Las Vegas circus style show, and the music isn't great, some tracks are sleepy or just don't fit the action. Still very good. I'd recommend but take a star off. The performers are incredible. The women are remarkable, they hold their breath underwater for minutes. I think men are also amazing, all strong, athletic, aerobic skills and stuff. But the women are amazing. The stage is circular, so no bad seats. There are 3 entrances, very important for transitions. The theatre and stage are beautiful and the lighting is great. It's an amazing production, ticket price is reasonable for Vegas compared to O or Love. Wish there were more effects, like fire, more epic, but this isn't an error. Great show, very visual, entertaining.

Just saw this circus-style theater show in Vegas last week. I would recommend, but knock off one star. The story is a bit hard to keep up with and some music doesn't fit or is just plain dull for the action. But all the performers are amazing, with the athletic ability and the physiques and the cardio. The female performers are so good. She stays underwater for a few minutes. I think the theater and stage were really beautiful. Both are circular, so your view is really good. They use 3 entrances to the stage, all around the edge. They become pretty important at the big transitions. The setting, the light, the whole place, it's all very beautiful. Very beautiful. The prices are quite reasonable. Reasonable compared to other Vegas shows. The “O” or the “Love” show or stuff like that. I really did wish it had some more spectacular effects. More fire, but I don't think that's a massive problem. It's just an entertaining, very visually beautiful show. I would recommend.

remote work is heralded as the panacea. but it's overblown for jrs still learning to code. My own experience. I mentored 5 jrs over 2 years.

Jrs don't really want ticket flow or documentation or meetings. they want to sit in on design conversations, see how people debug stuff, or ask questions before confusion takes hours of their day. This type of interaction is something that can happen organically in office. For remote work, you need to know what is the right time to cut in, or set up a call or say, "hi let's talk about this issue" something that you might not even fully understand. It's a skill to have before you have a chance to learn it, which is kind of tough.

I've seen the feedback issue. I think it's an issue in remote. Short comments on code review feel like the final word, instead of a learning opportunity. It takes longer, so it has less momentum. I've seen that with my own jrs, typically improved faster with in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, etc. easy access to seniors. I'm not trying to force offices and anti flexibility. I think remote work can be great for self driven devs, but for jrs, proximity is a booster that gives confidence, context, and instincts. So it can really be a drag on junior development to send jrs off with a laptop and a calendar. It can result in less good technical leadership in the future.

We are told remote is going to fix everything. Been mentoring five junior engineers for two years and I feel that it's been overblown. For juniors learning to write code. It's very hard to be a junior developer and you have to be self-driven and self motivated and self-aware. The jrs are usually very eager to learn. And they don't need tickets or docs or meetings. They need to listen to design conversations to see how other folks are debugging things and they need to ask questions so they don't get lost. So they have hours of confusion. And that kind of interaction usually happens in an office and it happens naturally. In remote work, you need to know the right time to cut in or set up a call and explain a problem you might not even understand yet. And that's a tough skill. I've seen the feedback issues with remote. Short comments on code review can feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. And it takes longer to see the code and give feedback and then get back to it. So the momentum is not as good. For my jrs, they did learn more if they had pairing in person and whiteboard and stuff, and seniors available. I don't see this to be against flexibility. I think remote work for self-driven devs is great. For jrs, it's just not as good, and the proximity is a booster. Gives you confidence, context and instincts. So when you send jrs to work remote with just a laptop and a calendar, I think that it'll make junior development a bit more of a drag. Which makes me think we'll see less good technical leaders in the future.

The mixer had been humming for hours. Steady drone and it vibrates through the soles of Elias’s boots. It was 3:17 AM and a lot of flour dust just hangs in the air, almost like snow, catching the harsh fluorescent light. The sourdough loaves were out on the wooden boards and they still had pale soft crusts that hadn’t been put in the oven. His hands were sticky from dough and sweat, he wiped them on his apron. He went to the front counter to check the lock. He always does, a ritual, born of paranoia. Then I saw it. The History of Salt. It’s a hardback and the spine was cracked, the blue spine. It came every Thursday for 6 weeks and is always placed on the glass case by the unsold cinnamon rolls. It didn’t have any library stamp, the bakery isn’t a branch of the municipal system. He picks it up, the cover felt cold. Opens the book, he was expecting blank pages, a forgotten bookmark. But a folded square of lined notebook paper had slipped out and it had landed on the counter. He unfolded it and the handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension. He stared at the words for a bit. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. He looked at his own hands, red knuckled and dusted white. He closed the book, put it back on the glass, aligned the spine perfectly with the edge. Then he turned off the overhead light above the display and left the book in shadow.

The industrial mixer just hummed this low steady drone, it vibrates through the soles of elias boots. Flour dust floating in the air caught by the harsh fluorescent light like suspended snow. 3:17 AM. Those sourdough loaves on wooden boards, the crusts are still pale and soft, waiting for final bake. He wiped hands on his apron which was stiff from dough and sweat. he moved to front counter to check the lock, a ritual more out of paranoia than need.

There it was. The History of Salt. Hardback, the blue spine cracked near the hinge. It had been showing up every Thursday for six weeks, placed just on the glass display next to the cinnamon rolls. no library stamp, it didn't belong here. It isn't a municipal system branch. he picked it up. cover felt cold. He opened it, was expecting blank pages or maybe some forgotten bookmark. But this folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out and landed on the counter with a soft tap.

He unfolded it. The writing was jagged, pressed really hard into the fiber. You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension. Elias just looked at the words. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. He looked at his hands, red knuckled, dusted white. He closed the book. He put it back on the glass, aligned the spine to the edge just right. Then he turned off the overhead light on the display and left the book in shadow.

I think Apple deserves a mention based on my own experience. My school only let middle and high schoolers use Apple stuff. Even though they cost about twice as much as PC options, the machines broke around once a month. I never once dropped my laptop but needed the hard drive replaced like 5 times over 4 years, and had to reinstall the OS again and again. One extreme thing happened to a friend's MacBook Pro which literally caught fire while he was watching a movie and the smoke alarm went off. To make it worse, Apple support kept not being able to diagnose our problems, so they just backed up the computer, wiped it, and restored files.

I have complaints about iPhones too. I owned the first one, which always broke in strange ways. Apple seems to put out a new iPhone like every two months, and it just has a slightly better camera than the last. One fair point though, iPads are the best tablets right now, but Android tablets are going to catch up.

so I went to see Awakening at Wynn Las Vegas. it’s fine but not really the kind of show you build a Vegas trip around. I’ve been dragged to Vegas constantly since I was a kid, seen tons of shows before 21, so I have a pretty decent reference point.

the circular stage is genuinely smart, from basically any seat you get a decent view and that’s rare in these big theater productions. if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore there’s a deal, tickets are usually $125 but hotel guests get $99. that helps.

some acts are impressive, the performers are strong as hell, aerialists and acrobats etc. but a lot of the feats felt like stuff I’ve seen just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows.

the bigger issue is the story, or lack of it. it’s unclear, weak or basically nonexistent. I left not really knowing what the show was trying to say. and there’s just too much going on, too many visuals, moving pieces, every few seconds they’re doing a “wow” thing. I think if it were more restrained it would hit harder.

overall aside from the cool stunts, it was kind of average. I wasn’t blown away. not really anyone I was with either. friends did enjoy it so if you haven’t seen it maybe check it out, and with the deal it’s worth the trip to Vegas. But I wouldn’t see it again. wouldn’t pay full price again for sure. it tries to be the stereotypical huge flashy vegas spectacle and more is better. More just meant messier.

So, quick take on Awakening at Wynn Las Vegas. It is fine, but not something I would plan a trip around. I’ve been dragged to Vegas since I was small, saw a bunch of shows before I turned 21, so I know what these things can be.

Good news is the circular stage, which is pretty smart. No matter where you sit you can see everything and that is rare with these huge theatre shows. I stayed at Wynn so I had a good price for tickets, $99 instead of $125 because of a deal for hotel guests.

The performers are really good, and there are some amazing acrobats and aerialists. But a lot of the stunts are stuff I’ve seen in Cirque shows too. That is the problem. The story isn’t that good. Not so good. I just don’t know what it’s trying to say. And there’s too much going on at once, just too much, way too many visuals, way too many moving pieces and too many things trying to say wow. A much more constrained show would have been much more effective. It’s just a really good acrobatic show, nothing else. Average. No one with me was really impressed, we all thought it was pretty average. But some of my friends did like it. So if you’ve never seen it before, go see it and you should get the same deal for $99. But I wouldn’t see it again for $125. For me it’s a classic Vegas big flashy show where more equals better, but more just means messier.

Said she was manager, told us she's built boards every day since hired, and on bad days she could be annoyed with customers and other people. So the build then, took about 90 minutes. I thought it would be 15. She actually stripped two bolts and put them back on in a way she seemed like she was gonna sell it later to a new customer. In the end she got her brother and another employee who she said was manager as well to finish/assist it. No apology. Zumiez lost our future business. It crushed my heart.

So yesterday we went back to Zumiez for the remaining board equipment and we got the skateboard. It started really well as my friends brother and I were chatting with a female staff member. She introduced herself as a manager, saying she's been putting skates together every day for as long as she's been working there. bought a mechanical keyboard second-hand for 38 dollars and it has been a chaotic ride. Seller's communication was terrible. I asked them what switches so I asked them before buying and they took a full week to respond with a one word response. By then I had already taken a gamble and ordered it. As for the board itself, it's definitely well-loved. Space bar has an incredibly annoying rattle to it like a loose lego. E key repeats sometimes so I get a lot of typos like theee instead of the lol. However it does feel really good. I love typing on it. Really like the feel of it. Tactile, feels really good. It's really good to pound out work email, the long agonizing kind of things. And I even thought about returning it. But I just decided not to. To ship back this thing which is pretty heavy and costs $38 and I'd have to pay shipping and it's not worth the trouble. So I've become pretty fond of it. Even I'm not a fan of its flaws. But if you don't mind the diying a little and the occasional letter typing twice or something, it's a good buy and I think that's the price I got it.

got this mechanical keyboard second hand for 38 dollars and it has been a wild ride, really chaotic but decent all the same. The seller was a nightmare to deal with, I wrote to ask what kind of switches then they did not reply for a full week and when they did it was just one word. By then I had already just gambled on it. The actual board, its well loved, space bar rattles so badly it sounds like a broken lego piece, and the e key repeats sometimes which leads to funny mistakes, theeee. But heres the thing, I genuinely really love using it. The tactile feedback is very good, and is actually very nice for mashing out long and painful work emails. Considered sending it back, but it is a slab of plastic and its heavy so returning it was not worth the hassle. Kept it, and even have grown to like the flaws a lot. If you are ok with doing a bit of do it yourself tweaking and having a double letter now and then, its a great deal.

travelers beware of Turkish Airlines. I had Harbin to Beijing domestic on a domestic line then Turkish Beijing to Istanbul. Harbin flight was delayed and I missed the connection. At the Turkish desk no one took responsibility or helped with rebook, I spent the night at airport. Next morning when I asked for a ticket staff told me flights overbooked and it could take days to get to Istanbul unless I paid business class. I needed Istanbul so I had no choice, accepted. Fuming and in disbelief.

Turkish airlines needs to be careful with travelers. I booked Harbin to Beijing domestic, then from Beijing to Istanbul, but Harbin was delayed, so I missed the connection. The booth at the airport didn't help, nobody even apologized, and told me flight was overbooked and would take days to get to Istanbul or I pay for business class. Had to accept it because I needed to go to Istanbul. I'm so mad, I just can't believe it. I spent the night at airport.

The float valve controls filling. A buoyant float is connected to the valve. If the water drops the float sinks and opens the valve so water goes in. Then as the water rises the float rises and gradually closes the valve. At the set level the valve shuts off. Filling stops. Two ordinary causes of overflow. Debris or mineral buildup where the valve can't close fully. Or the float has been misadjusted too high, meaning the valve closes only after it already overflowed.

float valves are really simple, just a float and a valve. water drops and the float goes down, opens the valve so the trough fills up. it starts closing the valve as water rises and when it reaches the level the fill stops. it does overflow sometimes but its rare. when it happens though 2 main reasons. stuff like sand or mineral buildup stops the valve from closing 100% so it doesn't fully close and water still drips in. or the float is set too high so the valve only closes after it's already overflowing.

So it works like this. Its a gravity siphon and air pressure does it. Its a tube that has to be filled with water and creates a continuous column. And the column has to span an elevated barrier. So the intake side has to be longer than the outlet. And gravity pulls it down the longer leg toward the lower container, and it will be a partial vacuum or reduced pressure on the top of the siphon. And atmospheric pressure pushing on the water level of the source will push more liquid in. And to get enough pressure and flow, it needs to be lower than the water level of the source. So if it was higher or level, gravity would not pull it down enough to overcome the lift on the other side. So it works because the weight of the column of water that's going down is heavier than the other leg. Air will break up this process. So when air bubbles get in there, it will break up the cohesive chain of water molecules, and then it will equalize the pressure on the inside of the tube with the atmosphere outside, so it stops. So it will fail until it's re-primed and re-filled.

So a siphon basically moves water between containers using gravity and atmospheric pressure to push liquid over a high barrier. The whole thing has to start by filling the tube with water for a continuous column. Once its going, gravity yanks the water down the descending leg, the longer leg, into the lower container. This downward movement lowers the pressure at the top of the siphon, creates a partial vacuum. Then air pressure presses down on the source container, forcing more liquid up the rising, shorter leg to fill the vacuum.

The out end has to be lower than the source water level, it needs to be. The force is the weight of the different water columns. If the exit is same level as the source or higher, gravity cant pull it down hard enough to push more water up the intakeside. The net pull is only there when the going down column is heavier than the going up column.

Air getting into the tube messes the whole process up. Its breaking the continuous liquid chain. Water molecules have to be in a solid chain, air bubbles separate them and break the chain, which means equal pressure with outside atmosphere. And pressure difference is what powers flow. When air gets in, the siphon stops. You gotta re-prime the tube with all liquid.

Found the sourdough again, second rise, Thursday once more. Its on the flour bin, the count of montecristo, Richmon public library stamp on it. I honestly don't know how they get in, door is super squeaky and all. Whatever, its 3am and I'm half baked with caffeine and yeast. But tonight, there was a scrap of yellow paper sticking out like a dog ear. Wiped my hands on my apron, white flour smudge left on the dark apron, and pulled the note out, its page 142, please. I think they're watching the drop box now, frantic spiky handwriting. Then a cold draft went through the kitchen, smelled like wet asphalt, rain about to hit. Looked out the front windows, nothing but my own tired face in the reflection. Didn't open it. Tucked the note back in the book. Slid it into a brown pastry bag, folded the top twice to seal it up.

My sourdough was on its second rise when I saw the book. Again. It's always a Thursday and always right on the flour bin and always a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp on it. Don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing, but at 3AM my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine. Tonight a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. So I wiped my hands on my apron, left a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth, and pulled the note out. Page 142. It's this frantic, spiky handwriting. They're watching the drop box now. I think they're watching it. There was this cold draft through the kitchen smelling like wet asphalt and rain. I looked toward the dark windows, it was just me looking back at myself. I didn't open the book, I put the note back between pages and put the novel in a brown pastry bag. Folded the top down twice to seal it.

Got this used mechanical for $38 and honestly it's worth about $38, maybe a bit more.

Flaws, start there. The spacebar rattles. Its a loose hollow clatter every time I thumb it, like nudging a tray of cutlery. Stopped noticing it in day time, but at late night it sounds louder than it has any right to. E key also repeats itself sometimes. So "meeting" becomes "meeeting." Happens maybe once every few paragraphs, often enough that I keep proofreading.
I asked what switches it had before buying. Communication with the seller was slow. The reply came a week later, after it arrived. Brown switches for the record.

But here's the surprising part. Genuinely comfortable. Keys are cushioned and satisfying, can write long emails without my wrist complaining. More than my old flat laptop keyboard lets me do.
Considered returning it but didnt see the point. It stays, rattling, repeating, quietly making up for it.
Three stars.

Paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard and I'd say I got about $38 worth maybe a little more. Lets do the flaws. Space bar rattles not a gentle click but a loose hollow clatter like a tray of cutlery when my thumb hits it. I don't notice during the day, but in the evenings it's worse. The E key will repeat and type meething like meeeting. Every few paragraphs. But the good part? Its super comfortable. It has a cushion feel to it that's very nice, lets type long emails and my wrists are happy. The laptop keyboard before was awful flat, not as good at all, and with this no complaints about wrists. Had a thought to send it back but didn't want the hassle. So keeping it. It works, has some rattle, the repeat issue, but works and earns its $38. 3 stars.

Good evening everyone. So, Tom has been such an exceptionally reliable guy and we are celebrating today. I've been following his life for a long time. He had to room with me in a bunk bed until he turned 14, so I've witnessed the snoring, witnessed the fights over who gets the top bunk. He is a type of brother who is loyal, who is generous, who is willing to go a completely unreasonable distance to save you from your own stupidity. For instance I forgot to bring my passport, and Tom made the 6 hour drive to get it to me. That's just him. And I am very happy you've found someone who loves you the same way we do. But unlike me, they decided to room with you on a voluntary basis.

Old school attendance registers are useful for historians trying to reconstruct daily life which is usually missing from official narratives. They show who showed up or who didn't, how regular their attendance was, and sometimes why they were off. From this historians can sort out seasonal work demands or illness or bad weather, poverty, family stuff, migration or some local emergency. The registers also let you see differences in gender, age, neighborhood or social class, which helps explain how school fit into work, household routines and community expectations. Over many years, these records show what changed in schooling habits and public health, but there is a limitation. They only show what the school chose to write down. They barely say anything about what the children actually experienced, and absences can be misreported or incomplete or just reflect some assumptions the teacher had. So really they only get any actual use when you go over them with some other sources.

Old school attendance registers are useful to historians because you can look back and see daily life which usually isn't in official accounts. They show who was there or not, how often kids came, and sometimes why they missed school. From this stuff you can tell things like seasonal work, illness, bad weather, poverty, or local emergencies, and see differences by gender or age or neighborhood or class. You can figure out how education worked alongside work and household routines. Looked at over several years you can see the changes. But a big issue is the registers only show what the school decided to put down. They will not explain in detail how the kids actually experienced things. Absences might get misreported, or left out, or written according to the teacher's own assumptions. Its best to use them side by side with other sources.

Every Thursday morning at 2:17, Mara would find that library book on the bakery's back step. Same one every time, A Field Guide to North American Moths, the county library sticker worn ghost-pale on the spine, and it had this little bit of flour worked into the jacket, like the book had been using it. She'd returned it twice but the librarians just smiled at her, too politely, so by the third week she'd left it out next to her rye starter and kept quiet. Tonight it was raining and the droplets were ticking against the alley door. The ovens were just breathing. She was shaping croissants then, pressing butter into the dough with her palms, and the back door latch made that little click, the guilty one. But nobody was there. Just the book, dry as bone, sat on the wet concrete. She wiped her hands on the apron and opened it up. There was a slip of paper between Luna Moth and Promethea, folded once. The note said, "Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I'm sorry about the crumbs." She looked out at the alley, at the dented milk crates, steam coming off the drains. For a second the city felt enormous, then it didn't. She tore a corner off her order pad and wrote that the cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then she tucked the note inside the book, put it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

I was curious about the stability of various folded cardboard bridge models, so we did this classroom project. Students used just cardboard, and they made short-beam ones, arch-inspired ones, and triangle folds. We tried to use the same materials, same width, same length, keep things as consistent as possible. We placed each bridge between two supports, added weight gradually, and see what happens, when it bends, tips, collapses. This was all handmade, limited tests, we did not do multiple runs, we had it only in the classroom. So we cannot treat it as an engineering data. Just as a classroom project, but the triangle fold seems to be more stable. It's not that it's completely rigid, but it appears more stable, and the different shapes make a big difference, geometry of fold.

this classroom project looked at the stability of folded cardboard bridge designs. they built short beam, arch-inspired, and triangular-fold bridges with the same cardboard, keeping length and width close as possible. then put them between two supports and added weights bit by bit and watched for bending tipping or collapse. the project was limited by everything being handmade, not many trials, classroom conditions so you cant read too much into it or treat the results as engineering data. but the triangular-fold ones seemed to hold weight much more steadily then the others. it does seem like fold geometry can influence stability.

I've been stuck at 23C and it's so very stuffy in my apartment. Temperature is just part of how a room feels, and we're talking about 18 to 27 degrees which is pretty comfortable, maybe for most people at least. My room feels super stuffy though. So humidity has a big part to play in stuffiness. When humidity is high it is difficult to evaporate moisture from skin, making air feel heavy, stale. Air flow is another factor, because low airflow will cause CO2, odour, heat to stay near occupant. And ventilation is also important. Poor ventilation will make a space feel stuffy. I have air con but it's making it worse, but at least it's making it more comfortable. You can open the window, use a fan, or turn on ventilation to make it feel fresher.

So I don't think it works out. A room can feel stuffy even when it's actually a reasonable temperature because you've got humidity slowing the moisture leaving your skin and that can make it feel heavy. Not just temp, it can be very close. And poor ventilation traps all that CO2, all the odour, heat. It's just trapped, it's not moving and not dispersing. So you can have air conditioning and it can be a cool temperature, but it doesn't help if the humidity is really high or the air isn't moving. You need air movement. You open the windows, you can run a fan, you can run ventilation. You need to move the air and hopefully lower the humidity.

My office is in the building. But I also work remotely and I think the best way to explain it is like this, if you go remote, if you go hybrid, you'll miss out on the junior's experience. You get told remote work is a win for everybody and I don't think it is. I've mentored 5 junior engineers for the last 2 years, and what they need is not tickets or docs or a set of scheduled meetings. What they need is to get in on design arguments, watch somebody else get through a nasty bug, get answers before a little uncertainty snowballs. You get all of that for free in an office. If you go remote, and I'll say, it's not that bad but you have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call set up, explain a problem they don't quite get yet. That's a pretty steep ask for someone who hasn't been there.

And I've seen the setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review ends up reading like a final judgment, lag on getting answers kills forward motion. The 5 engineers I worked with moved ahead a lot quicker when they could pair up in person, work through things on a whiteboard, and actually get hold of seniors. None of this means you should scrap flexibility. It works for people who can direct their own efforts, that's no problem. For a beginner, being around people is how they pick up confidence, context, and judgment they're going to need. If you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar, you'll end up with a very weakened technical leadership down the road.

rain gauges are a bit basic, they just collect falling rain, open and measure. so you get depth mm or inch. basically it would be that depth would have covered flat earth if not drain or evaporate or soaked. many gauges have a funnel with a large opening, then a smaller measure tube, and water rise higher, you get more accurate small rainfall, but scale is calibrated to area ratio and show true depth. wind can really make your reading off, so wind can push rain drop past the opening and cause under count. evaporation or splashing before reading also mess up the reading a bit, that's how it works

Rain gauges are pretty simple, just collects rain falling into a known area opening, then it reports depth in mm or inches. The depth tells you how much water would have covered flat ground if nothing had soaked or evaporated. Usually there's a funnel on top with a wide mouth that dumps into a slim tube. With the same volume going into a small tube, even small amounts go higher so it's easy to measure. The tube scale factors in the funnel area ratio so you get the true depth. Wind screws up stuff though, it carries the raindrops past the opening so you're undercounting. The water evaps before you get to read it or you can't get an accurate measurement. And then you get splashing before reading.

Old attendance registers are pretty valuable stuff for historians who want to reconstruct how everyday life worked. They meticulously track students being there, and this shows up patterns like seasonal work on farms, local epidemics, bad weather. A sudden dip in attendance could mean some flu or it's harvest time so kids have to work on the farm, so education versus economic needs gets complicated. And if certain groups just never seem to show up that points to some social inequalities in society or some cultural attitudes towards school. So this is good data, but you have to use these things with care because of administrative inconsistency or deliberate falsification. Headmasters and teachers might have doctored the attendance numbers to meet funding requirements or to avoid scrutiny from the education authority. The data isn't always the truth and registers rarely explain why kids aren't in. And that makes it hard to tell for sure what happened, you have to do detective work, cross-reference with other sources. So they're a useful way of understanding how communities work but always use with care and compare them with other sources.

Old attendance registers are pretty valuable for historians who want to understand what daily life looked like in past communities. They're just notes on which kids showed up or not. If you look at patterns and see drops around certain seasons, like harvest time, you can start to connect dots like flu outbreaks, or bad weather, or work on farms taking kids away from school. You also get info on groups that never really bother to show, which often means there's a bigger social issue or cultural thing. The thing is, you have to be careful reading these. Teachers or headmasters have been caught fiddling with numbers so they could pass the funding requirements or dodge inspection. The register doesn't say why a kid didn't show, so historians have to cross-reference with other historical evidence to figure out the social structure.

A float valve connects the trough to a pressurized water line. A buoyant float, usually a plastic ball or block, rests on the water surface, attached to a lever. So if the cattle drink and the level drops, the float sinks, tilting the arm and pulling the plunger or washer away from the seat, so water then flows in.
When water rises, the float lifts. That pushes the plunger back, against the seat, closing the opening up to the set level, and once there the flow stops.
Overflow happens most from debris fouling the washer or just wearing out the washer or seat. Also you can get it when the float gets punctured and waterlogged, so it doesn't lift enough.
